title: the symbol on the flag
hookLine: the symbol on the flag outside the gurdwara, on car windows and pendants: what each piece means
carry: the inner and the outer, held together
last: WAHEGURU · LANGAR · THE TURBAN · PANJ PYARE · ARDAS · SIKH

lines: ON THE FLAG. ON THE CAR. ON THE ARM.
cards: It's on the flag outside the gurdwara. On car window stickers, pendants, gates, phone cases and forearms. A circle, a straight double-edged sword through the middle, and two curved swords wrapped around the outside.
Plenty of people could draw it from memory. Fewer could say what each piece means.

teach.b: It's called the Khanda, after the sword in the middle. A khanda is a straight, double-edged sword, the very kind of blade that stirred the water at the first initiation, with the five from day four.
Sikhs often read its two edges as the power to cut truth from falsehood.

teach.h: THE CIRCLE — NO BEGINNING, NO END.
teach.b: Around it, the circle, the chakkar. It was once a real steel ring, thrown in battle, but in the emblem it's read as the one with no beginning and no end, like the kara on the wrist.
Then the two curved swords on the outside.

teach.h: MIRI AND PIRI — WORLD AND SPIRIT.
teach.b: They're usually read as miri and piri: the outer life and the inner life, the world and the spirit, held together. The sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind, wore two swords to say exactly that.
So at the center there's no crown and no face: just a blade that cuts lies.

teach.h: THE FLAG SAYS: SHELTER AND A MEAL.
teach.b: The flag it flies on, the Nishan Sahib, is saffron or blue, on a tall pole, so anyone, from far off, can find shelter and a meal.
And at Vaisakhi, the spring harvest festival and the day the five stood up, many gurdwaras lower the flag, wash the pole and dress it in fresh cloth.

how: The Khanda appears on the Nishan Sahib, the saffron or blue flag that flies on a tall pole at gurdwaras; at Vaisakhi many gurdwaras renew the flag and the pole's cloth, and Sikhs celebrate the harvest and the Khalsa's founding with Nagar Kirtan processions.

games.q: what's inside the symbol — tap the pairs.
p: the double-edged sword at the center
the circle, without beginning or end

s: the Khanda is a symbol of war
Sikhs read it as truth cut from falsehood, the one without end, and world and spirit held together.
a khanda stirred the water at the first initiation in 1699
the double-edged sword that gives the emblem its name.
Vaisakhi is only a harvest festival
it's the spring harvest and the day the Khalsa was founded in 1699: both.

games.q: you're becoming the sixth Guru. you're offered the old signs of the role. what do you ask for?
o: two swords: one for the world, one for the spirit.
games.why: tradition says Guru Hargobind wore two swords, miri and piri. they're the two curved swords on the Khanda.

games.q: build the Khanda, from the center out.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, think of your outer life: work, bills, the list of things to do. On the second, your inner life: what you hope for, what you love.
On the third, hold both at once, the way the two swords hold the circle.

wordCard.voice: The Khanda. A double-edged sword, a circle without end, and two swords for world and spirit. Seventh word: a week's worth.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: a straight, double-edged sword, and the emblem named after it.

carryVoice: Your line: the inner and the outer, held together. That's week one: seven words, and what's inside each. Tomorrow, the hands nobody sees.
